new_statements.quote: In Zambian languages, in contrast, syllables are more or less evenly stressed, i.e. they are pronounced with almost the same degree of prominence or force. In some languages, however, (e.g. Cewa) the penultimate syllable seems to be pronounced with slightly greater force than the rest of the syllables in the same word. [...] In any case, independent of the lengthening of vowels, stress in Zambian languages does not distinguish words from each other in meaning. A characteristic feature of all Zambian languages is that each of their syllables carries tone. [...] There are only two contrastive tones in Zambian languages, high and low, which serve to distinguish between words which are otherwise identical in all other respects. (scanned text layer; 'vv'->'w', 'ali'->'all', 'syilable'->'syllable' normalized)

A characteristic feature of ali Zambian languages is that each of their syllables carries tone.. only tvvo contrastive tones in Zambian languages, high and low' - A's quote is this text with the scanned vv->w, ali->all, syilable->syllable normalisations it declared. Table 1:1 p. 21 (lines 1084-1088) lists 'Toka 5,564 6,430 11,994 0.3' and 'Leya 3,722 4,152 7,874 0.2' under Group K (Tonga);…
new_statements.relation_note: Two-tone (H/L) systems in all Zambian languages; no contrastive stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: All Zambian (Bantu) languages are tone languages with two contrastive tones (H, L) on every syllable; stress is not distinctive - syllables are evenly stressed, with at most slight penult prominence in some languages (Cewa) attributable to penultimate vowel lengthening.
new_statements.exceptions: Cewa-type slight penult force tied to penultimate lengthening (stated p. 63-64 as a rule of Eastern Province and some North-Western Province languages, not of the Tonga group); contextual tone changes (downdrift, H->L alternations) illustrated from Bemba and Lambya.
new_statements.identity_note: Country-wide generalization: the authors state explicitly that in these sections they describe 'patterns common among all Zambian languages as illustrated by the languages which we studied' (p. 62); Toka (11,994 speakers, 1969 census) and Leya (7,874) are listed as members of the Tonga language group in Table 1:1 (p. 21) but were not among the languages individually studied; the statement therefore covers Toka-Leya only as part of 'all Zambian languages'. Zimbabwean Dombe is outside its scope. Not in Glottolog's domb1246 list; Routledge 2017 reprint DOI 10.4324/9781315106786-4. | tong1318 (A's work 4, re-reported because the full text does carry a prosodic statement): Valley Tonga of Siavonga vs Plateau Tonga of Mazabuka, Monze, Choma, Kalomo; Toka, Leya, Livingstone, Kazungula never occur; sec. 1.1 lists Zimbabwean Tonga areas incl. 'Victoria Falls' only as hearsay, and the recommendations call for a future cross-border study of those areas.

new_statements.quote: (pp. 264-265, sec. 3.3.1) The following observations on tone are concentrated on PI, because our data for other lects are limitedto citation forms. In this limited context no variation has been observed within the core lects but the relation with Sp and Ttis complex and the tonal reliability of the data is suspect ... Like vowel and consonant tone plays an integral part in the phonology of the Tonga lects. It is used to distinguish words which otherwise have identical segmental forms. || (p. 29) In the present study Plateau, Valley, Toka, Ila, Lenje and Soli will be termed the 'core lects' because as we shall show in Chapter 3 these lects share certain sound changes among themselves such as merging the long and short vowels of PT to short (3.2) and also in having similar tone patterns at least in citation forms (3.3). || (p. 63, on Toka, Valley, Plateau) Differences at the tonal level is negligible at least if we look at the surface tonal patterns of lexical items in isolation
new_statements.citation: Hachipola, Simooya Jerome. 1991. A historico-comparative study of Zambian Plateau Tonga and seven related lects (Valley, Toka, Ila, Lenje, Soli, Supiya, Totela). PhD thesis, School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London. 563 pp. doi:10.25501/SOAS.00028969

new_statements.relation_note: First-hand tone-marked Toka data and an explicit statement that tone is integral to the phonology of the Tonga lects incl. Toka, with negligible tonal difference from Plateau Tonga; nothing on stress/accent for Toka
new_statements.rule_in_words: Toka, with the other 'core' Tonga lects, is described as tonal: High vs Low tone with lexical and grammatical function; Toka surface tones in citation forms show no variation from Plateau Tonga; tones (H/L) are marked impressionistically on the c. 650-item Toka wordlist in the Appendix. No stress or accent statement is made for Toka: the accentual (Goldsmith) analysis is discussed for Plateau Tonga only, and the 'penultimate prominence' remark on p. 277 concerns Supiya and Totela, not the core lects.
new_statements.exceptions: Appendix item 416 'monkey' (and cross-ref. 526): 'The tone pattern in Vy and Tk differs from that of the other cognates. This is one of the few cases where the tone patterns differ'; author calls all tone marks tentative ('The tones should be taken as tentative pending further study', p. 277) since non-Plateau data are citation forms only
new_statements.identity_note: Toka is a Glottolog dialect of domb1246 (Toka-Leya-Dombe); data elicited 1987 from Toka speakers of Zimba, Kalomo district, Zambia; author states Leya and Toka are 'almost indistinguishable' and uses Toka for both; Dombe (Zimbabwe) not mentioned [name in source: Toka (abbreviated Tk); 'the Leya and Toka are generally known as Toka-Leya' - Leya treated as near-identical to Toka but not separately sampled; pages p. 2 (abstract), p. 29 (core lects), p. 34 (informants: Toka, Zimba, Kalomo district), pp. 51-52 (lects included/excluded), p. 63, pp. 264-265 (sec. 3.3.1 Tone), p. 277, Appendix wordlist (c. 650 items, tone-marked, Tk column)]
